summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national framework, which the parent record carries; this assessment covers only what is specific to the island.

Detention is the documented risk area. French prison rules govern detention in Guadeloupe, and a BuzzFeed News report of January 2018 found that the placement of trans women follows the legal gender recorded on their incarceration papers, which may not correspond to the person's presentation; in practice assignment is said to weigh the individual's best interests, with individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings used where possible. The national preventive mechanism (CGLPL) issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, finding that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, drawing on some 40 referrals since 2010.

Practical support on the island is limited but real. Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, offering reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities, driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations. The opening was attended by the visiting national minister Aurore Bergé, who announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted for overseas territories. Community organisations including Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025.

Community organising is described as advancing. An interview with Leïla of Secret's Out in September 2023 reported that community members increasingly reconcile their lives with their orientation, with activism described as progressing after sister island Martinique; the interview also featured Prisca Melyon-Reinette of Amalgame Humani's.
tangentialFactors:
The national legal layer that reaches Guadeloupe includes a conversion therapy ban published on 1 February 2022 carrying two years' imprisonment and/or a €30,000 fine, and the law of 31 December 2004 criminalising homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment. These are national provisions restated here only as context for what applies on the island.

Reported homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults across France rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018; no Guadeloupe-specific breakdown of such incidents was identified in the sources.
localsOnly:
Residents use the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened 24 April 2024, as the island's principal reception, support and orientation point for matters of identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversity. The centre is run by a federation of Guadeloupean associations rather than a state body.

Local organisations active on the island include Secret's Out, Queer Gang, Lovo Nova and Amalgame Humani's. Secret's Out's leadership has described a gradual shift in which community members reconcile their lives with their orientation, with activism on Guadeloupe following a path opened in Martinique.

Legal gender recognition, name changes, marriage and identity documents are handled under the French procedures described in the national record; the registry office and court channels apply here as in the metropole.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Guadeloupe-specific incident of violence against a trans person, with date and outcome, was identified in the sources; the violence figures cited are national French statistics without an overseas breakdown.

Whether the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion handles trans-specific casework, and what reception capacity it has, is not sourced.

The measures announced by Aurore Bergé during her April 2024 visit are described in general terms as adapted structures for overseas territories; their specific content and implementation status on the island are unresolved in the sources.

Whether the CGLPL's 2021 findings on places of deprivation of liberty have been acted on in Guadeloupe's own detention facilities is not sourced.
